thread.title: Will Americans pay companies to protect their personal data? Here’s their answer - MarketWatch

author: Kari Paul
title: Will Americans pay companies to protect their personal data? Here’s their answer - MarketWatch
text:
Americans want more control over their personal data — as long as it doesn’t come with a price tag.
The vast majority of Americans (80%) would like online services to collect less of their data, but only 26% would be willing to pay a monthly subscription fee in exchange for privacy, a survey published on Wednesday by Washington, D.C. privacy nonprofit Center for Data Innovation found.
In fact, more than 50% of the 3,240 adult internet users it surveyed were opposed to paying a subscription fee to see fewer ads.
The Center for Data Innovation formulates and promotes public policies “designed to maximize the benefits of data-driven innovation,” according to its LinkedIn profile . It’s a research center within the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, which includes representatives from Apple AAPL, +0.40% Oracle ORCL, +1.04% Microsoft MSFT, +0.65% Amazon AMZN, +0.49% and Google GOOG, +0.75% on its board . Funding for the organization comes from corporations, foundations, governments and individuals.
It’s probably not surprising that people would be unwilling to pay for products they see on a website — and also pay to prevent their data being collected. It’s probably not surprising that people would be unwilling to pay for products they see on a website — and also pay to for more privacy and prevent their personal data being collected. For many consumers, that may feel like a double-dip by companies, privacy experts say.
What’s more, the practice of collecting users’ personal data can feel invasive, especially when users see ads for certain products, like baby cribs and maternity clothing , show up across the web after they’ve been searching for related terms online.
Companies say when websites know consumers’ likes and desires, they can meet them more efficiently, which saves consumers time. A Facebook spokesman told MarketWatch this week consumers often complain about being served irrelevant ads, and that the company is on a mission to show people “better ads” while protecting people’s information.
However, those targeted advertisements comes at a high price: Facebook collects data on everything from users’ political leanings to their “multicultural affiliations,” and other consumer habits and pop culture “likes.”
Daniel Castro, the director of the Center for Data Innovation, explicitly favors people sharing their data in order to receive more targeted advertising. “Limiting personal data-collection would require trade-offs,” he said. “Sharing less data would reduce the services consumers have available to them, decrease the quality of services they enjoy, and limit the innovation that makes creating and improving these services possible.”
The privacy vs. data debate has become increasingly heated Others disagree. Congress is discussing privacy laws after recent high-profile scandals, including Facebook’s FB, +0.37% Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018, in which it was revealed the social-media platform was sharing user data with marketing firms that may have played a role in the 2016 election.
The debate over data versus privacy has come to the forefront of consumer advocacy, corporate marketing and lawmaking.
On Thursday, Apple AAPL, +0.40% chief executive officer Tim Cook said it is time for Congress to pass “comprehensive federal privacy legislation” and that the Federal Trade Commission should allow people to track and delete their data on demand.
“Technology has the potential to keep changing the world for the better, but it will never achieve that potential without the full faith and confidence of the people who use it,” he said.
Privacy groups came together on Wednesday to propose Congress to create a new Government Data Protection Agency. Privacy groups came together on Wednesday to propose Congress to create a new Government Data Protection Agency, which would supplant the Federal Trade Commission and have rule making authority.
This proposal was put forward by non-profits Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood, Center for Digital Democracy, Color of Change, Consumer Federation of America, Electronic Privacy Information Center, and Public Citizen.
Castro noted that “overly restrictive privacy legislation” would likely increase costs for companies, which would start charging consumers for subscriptions and raising the prices of existing subscriptions to compensate.
Others, however, have argued that consumers are the product for social-media companies and say they should be paid directly when they hand over their data .
Privacy scandals have not been good for business, either. Following its Cambridge Analytica incident, Facebook lost $120 billion in market value in July 2018.
Privacy and free services are not necessarily incompatible, said Terence Jackson, chief information security officer at Washington, D.C. security and privacy firm Thycotic. “The recent Facebook ‘breach of trust’ has made us reconsider the information that we share with these types of services,” he said.
“For there to be real change and accountability, we have to be a more informed consumer of these products, understand what we are opting into and then have to sense of mind to walk away from them if we are not comfortable with how our data will be used.”
